title: The Independent Artist's Marketing Guide: No Label, No Budget, No Problem
author: Sidney Swift
excerpt: A small-budget music marketing plan with content ideas, a suggested weekly schedule, relevant outreach, and practical ways to test AI.
body:
I talk to independent artists every week. The conversation usually goes the same way.

"I know I need to market my music. I just don't have the money to hire anyone. And I don't have the time to do it all myself."

You can start with a small budget and the tools you already have. The aim is a process you can sustain, with enough room to learn what your audience responds to.

This guide focuses on lower-cost ways to prepare content, build relationships, and organize release promotion. Check current tool pricing and limits before committing to a workflow.

## First, Stop Doing These Things

Start by removing work that does not support the audience or relationships you want to build.

**Do not buy fake followers.** Inflated counts obscure the audience you are actually reaching. Evaluate real listening, engagement, and relevant responses instead.

**Keep hashtags relevant.** Check current platform guidance and use tags that describe the content. A large tag count is not a substitute for a clear idea.

**Vary the story around the song.** Alongside listening links, share a performance, a useful detail, or the story behind the music.

**Avoid guaranteed-placement or artificial-streaming offers.** Review the provider and the platform’s current rules. A payment does not establish that a playlist has a real, relevant audience.

Then choose a manageable set of things to try.

## Start with the Tools You Have

Check whether your existing accounts can cover these jobs:

- **Artist dashboards:** profile updates, permitted submissions, and available analytics
- **A phone or camera:** raw performance and behind-the-scenes material
- **An editor:** the video and caption formats you need
- **A design tool:** reusable visual templates
- **A listening-link page:** a clear route to the release
- **An AI assistant:** selected drafts or research, subject to the product’s limits

Free tiers may cover some tasks, but usage, exports, scheduling, and other features can have limits or costs. Confirm them before building the plan around a tool.

Start with a setup you can use consistently, then pay for additional capabilities only when they solve a clear problem.

## Content Ideas to Test

These formats can start with material you record yourself. Their value depends on the idea, execution, and audience response.

### The Talking Head

Sit in front of your phone. Talk about something real. The story behind your song. An opinion about the industry. A lesson you learned. Something funny that happened at a gig.

A direct-to-camera story gives listeners a way to learn about the person behind the music. Compare it with other formats instead of assuming it will outperform a polished video.

Aim for 30-60 seconds. Strong hook in the first 2 seconds. Post on TikTok and Instagram Reels simultaneously.

### The Process Video

Film yourself making music. Not the polished "studio session" content. The real thing. Struggling with a lyric. Finding a chord progression. The moment a song clicks.

Process content can show how the music takes shape. Use it when the moment is interesting, rather than treating it as a signal that guarantees algorithmic reach.

### The Duet/Stitch

React to other artists' content. Put your spin on trending sounds. Stitch a video with your take on a music industry topic.

A relevant response or collaboration may introduce your work to new people. Another video’s view count does not establish how many of those viewers will see yours or become fans.

### The Collaboration Post

Find artists at your level (similar follower count, similar genre) and create content together. This can be as simple as a split-screen reaction to each other's music or a joint Instagram Live.

A well-matched collaboration can introduce each artist to a relevant new audience. Reach depends on audience overlap, engagement, and how the collaboration is promoted.

## A Suggested Weekly Schedule

Use this as a planning exercise. The timeboxes and post counts below are optional targets, not measured production times; adjust them to your material and review needs.

**Sunday (30 min):** Batch record 3-4 talking head videos and 1-2 process clips. Don't edit. Don't overthink. Just hit record.

**Monday:** Post talking head #1 (TikTok + Reels)

**Tuesday:** Post process video (TikTok + Reels)

**Wednesday:** Text post or carousel on Instagram (use your AI agent to generate this from your video content)

**Thursday:** Post talking head #2 (TikTok + Reels)

**Friday:** Post something personal — a story, a photo dump, a meme about your genre

**Saturday:** Engage. Spend 15 minutes commenting on other artists' posts, responding to your DMs, and interacting with fans.

That is a proposed mix of five posts in a week. Publish fewer if the material or available time does not support the plan.

An AI assistant can help develop additional drafts from approved material. Review them before adding them to a schedule, and confirm that your tools support the publishing steps you want.

## Promotion Tasks to Consider

### Playlist Pitching (Do It Yourself)

Look for playlists whose music and audience fit the release, then check whether and how they accept submissions.

Search by genre and related artists, listen to the playlist, and check the curator’s stated submission route. Audience size is one input; relevance and activity matter too.

An illustrative pitch to adapt:

"Hey [name], I'm [your name], an independent [genre] artist from [city]. I just released [song name] and think it could be a good fit for [playlist name]. It's in the vein of [comparable artist]. Here's the link: [Spotify link]. Thanks for listening either way."

Build a shortlist of relevant playlists, check each curator’s submission guidance, and track responses. Placements depend on fit and curator decisions; do not plan a campaign around a promised acceptance rate.

### Personal Outreach

Share a release with people for whom it is relevant and welcome. Use each curator’s or publication’s stated submission process rather than treating every social profile as an invitation to pitch.

4. Records approved submissions and responses

Use the playlist sources you are permitted to access to prepare a shortlist. Useful information may include:

- Genre and mood fit
- Recent additions and their dates
- Available audience or activity information
- Submission instructions
- Your own record of previous contact and responses

### 2. Personalized Pitch Generation

Each pitch references specific details:

> "Hi [Curator] — I noticed you added [Recent Track] to [Playlist Name] last week. [Artist]'s new track [Title] shares that [specific quality] — dreamy production with a driving rhythm section. It's been streaming well in [relevant market] since release, with [specific data point]. Think it could be a great fit alongside [comparable track already on the playlist]."

This is an illustrative draft. Replace the placeholders only with facts you have checked, and do not claim to have listened or researched something you have not.

### 3. Multi-Channel Delivery

Use the submission channel the curator specifies. An email address or social profile alone does not establish that pitches are welcome there.

Delivery can be part of a configured workflow, but it needs permitted access and approval of the recipient, channel, and message.

### 4. Response Tracking & Follow-Up

Keep a record of:
- Approved submissions and dates
- Responses and stated preferences
- Placements you can verify
- Any follow-up the curator requested
- Attribution limits: a placement after a pitch does not always establish that the pitch caused it

That record can help avoid duplicate or unwanted contact and inform later research. It does not guarantee that each campaign will perform better.

## Keep Useful History

The value of a maintained record is that the next campaign can use what the team has already learned.

Review that history for:
- Relevant past responses
- Changes in playlist focus or submission guidance
- Contacts who asked not to receive more pitches
- Details that have become outdated

AI and manual systems can both retain this information. Choose a process the team can keep accurate and current.

Coordinate playlist research with other work where the information is relevant:

- **Streaming data:** verify whether a particular audience or market is relevant to the pitch
- **Social activity:** use checked context without overstating traction
- **Release plans:** respect submission windows and asset availability
- **Fan communication:** share confirmed placements when appropriate

A useful pitch explains why the track fits. Include a growth claim only when you have evidence and the reporting period is clear.

1. **Confirm access:** identify permitted data sources and submission channels.
2. **Describe the track:** add genre, mood, artist context, and checked facts.
3. **Research and draft:** review a manageable shortlist and pitch batch.
4. **Approve delivery:** confirm recipients, content, and any configured sending tools.

Once you try to get AI systems to run real, multi-step work with real users, the problems show up quickly. Not in demos, but in retries, in edge cases, and in the second run that never happens because trust was lost the first time.

Meta just paid to avoid learning that lesson internally.

## What is Manus?

Most AI products look capable when the task is short and clean.

They struggle when the work stretches across time, tools, and decisions. Context degrades. Tool calls return partial output. The system technically completes the task, but the result isn't usable.

Manus focused on that layer.

It built an orchestration system designed to keep an agent coherent across longer jobs. If a tool fails, the system notices. If the task branches, it tracks where things left off. If something goes wrong halfway through, the job doesn't simply collapse.

That doesn't produce flashy demos. It produces systems people are willing to rely on more than once.

That reliability is what Meta bought.

Meta doesn't lack AI talent, compute, or research depth.

What it lacks is tolerance for the slow, awkward phase where execution systems actually get good. Orchestration-heavy products surface edge cases late. They require shipping things that feel unfinished. The progress shows up gradually, mostly as fewer problems rather than obvious wins.

That's a hard sell inside a large organization with quarterly expectations.

Buying Manus let Meta skip the most painful part of that curve and acquire a system that had already survived contact with real usage.

This wasn't an experiment. It was risk removal.

There's a common assumption that as models improve, everything else becomes interchangeable.

In practice, the opposite is happening.

Models are already good enough to decide what should happen next. The constraint has moved to execution. Staying coherent across steps. Handling failure without human cleanup. Producing outcomes that don't need to be redone.

That's the orchestration layer.

Meta paying billions for a company that concentrated almost entirely on that problem is a pricing signal. It shows where the difficulty still lives, and where value is quietly accumulating.

As software becomes easier to build, many teams default to adding AI features on top of existing products.

That works for bounded tasks.

It breaks down when work involves sequencing, judgment, and ownership across time. Someone still has to hold the job together. When no system does, execution depends on memory, follow-ups, and hero operators.

The companies that last treat reliability as part of the product itself, not something to clean up later.

_A&R, marketing, release management, and exec leadership should each have a default Recoup workflow_

Let's break down the details of each:

Quarter 1 - Email + SMS Clients.
--------------------------------

*   Morning brief: priorities + campaign opportunities.
    
*   Weekly release pulse: what’s moving, what’s not.
    
*   Alerting: spikes, influencer mentions, playlist adds, content ideas.
    

Meet people where they are. So far, Recoup has really only existed as a web app. Whenever an artist wants to use Recoup, they visit the website at [https://app.recoupable.dev](https://app.recoupable.dev) and start a new chat. While this is familiar for artists who already use ChatGPT or Grok, it is not ideal for retention. We observed that web-only usage was low in 2025.

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/2a2e0e15188b411cff8960e7d2785ca9ffb50bb1ad348fa10fea11266f27960b.png)

Artists and music label executives run their business on email. Artists are already familiar with making and taking booking opportunities via email. Music label employees show up at the office and the first thing they do is open their email. We can deliver Recoup directly into inboxes on a consistent basis and drastically reduce friction to engage. If Recoup's email and SMS presence add value consistently, we will build trust as a daily check-in point in enterprise label teams for finding and developing opportunities to grow their campaigns and careers.

Goal: make Recoup a daily habit.  
Ships: daily brief, weekly release pulse, alerts, reply-to-act workflows.  
Outcome: higher WAU/seat, faster action loops.

Quarter 2 - Media Generation.
-----------------------------

> _We’ll prioritize commercially safe outputs, repeatable templates, and team approvals._

Higgsfield helps storytellers produce high-quality, stylized content with true cinematic control. Artists and record labels need media assets for their next campaign. As we have worked with enterprise partners, we find that they use Higgsfield, in addition to Recoup. This creates a fractured workflow where campaign strategy and management are handled in Recoup while video generation happens in Higgsfield. In quarter 2, we will improve Recoup's media generation pipeline to be good enough for campaign work, tightly integrated with strategy and approvals.

Quarter 3 - Label Services.
---------------------------

In Q3 we’ll package our tools into role-based services (Research, Release Planning, Content Ops, CRM/Outreach) and expose them via API so enterprises can integrate Recoup into their internal systems.

Quarter 4 - Build your own Label.
---------------------------------

> _For enterprises, this means standardized internal playbooks and reusable agents across teams; for artists and developers, it means a customizable stack._

A rising tide raises all ships. The current music industry is private and proprietary. You win and keep your secrets to yourself. We want to build a better music industry. We believe open templates, agent recipes, integrations and SDKs while keeping enterprise features secure and supported will ultimately accelerate the benefit artist intelligence will have on the trajectory of artists. It's taken us 15 months to build the current Recoup stack. Now, we’re productizing the stack.

*   Record labels pick and choose their favorite flavors of label services without increasing headcount.
    
*   Artists build the label they've always dreamed of without selling any rights to their art.
    
*   Developers build variations of this tech we didn't think of.
    

If you run an enterprise label team and want to pilot Email + SMS agents in Q1, email agent@recoupable.dev.

title: Sandbox for Record Labels
author: Recoupable Team
excerpt: File system + bash for your mood boards, docs and rules.
body:
You open up gmail and send an email to agent@recoupable.dev

> Generate an image for Wiz Khalifa's active campaign.

A new sandbox is created with Wiz Khalifa's file system. Claude Code is running your prompt. It looks at the docs to find the details of the active campaign, including the images you've already generated for the campaign. It looks at your mood board to understand reference images of Wiz Khalifa and the campaign. Claude generates an image and adds it to the campaign folder. It replies to your email attaching the photo it generated. It updates the progress file for the campaign noting the details of the created image. The sandbox is destroyed.

The Problem
-----------

Why are sandboxes required? Couldn't record labels already do all of this with API endpoints and the Claude API? No, we couldn't. Simple APIs lack the following:

*   File System
    
*   Bash
    

Both are simple primitives which have existed since the first days of computing. APIs are great to trigger the creation of a sandbox. However, in serverless stacks like Cloudflare and Vercel, APIs lack both bash and the file system.

Bash
----

Bash is the command line. Bash is where Claude Code runs. Bash can read and write files, fetch web pages from urls, query APIs, open pull requests, basically anything you can do via a web page Claude Code can do via bash. However, bash is very powerful, it can run malicious commands which might corrupt your local file system or a shared system. By putting bash in a sandbox, we give Claude Code an isolated, untrusted, environment where it can execute tasks for your record label without corrupting your local computer. However, with Bash, we need a file system for files to be read from and written to.

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/f06c6398d753ed5b5b68ebdca48a4e4ebda46642438d51fe5b53ff87a40c0c43.png)

File System
-----------

File systems are where record labels get work done. It's what Claude Code directly reads / writes to with untrusted access. We give it a structure built for record labels with the following architecture:

*   `ORG.md` - Rules for my record label.
    
*   `moodboard/` - Reference media for Claude Code to create media which references the record label's style.
    
*   `media/` - Media created by Claude Code for the record label.
    
*   `workspaces/[workspaceName]/` - All files for a musician, or other workspace within your record label. A grouping of files.
    
    *   `WORKSPACE.md` - Rules for the musician.
        
    *   `moodboard/` - Reference media for Claude Code to create media which references the musician's style.
        
    *   `media/` - Media created by Claude Code for the musician.
        

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/f11dd7edf2f63e8935a8f77ff306f206e9f91e6e55b872afd5b9b82ff5e2c3af.png)

Other than that, the file system is yours to customize. You can add anything from marketing templates to social media data tracking sheets. The more you use your Sandbox, the more customized it becomes, the better it understands your active campaigns which leads to higher quality outputs.

Why not VPS?
------------

VPS is overkill. Sandbox provides just-in-time bash + filesystem.

> **Virtual Private Server** (VPS) is a virtualized, isolated server partition within a physical machine, offering dedicated resources (CPU, RAM, storage) and root access for improved performance, security, and control over shared hosting. It acts as an independent server, allowing users to run custom operating systems and applications, commonly using Linux or Windows. 

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/c2f70a8810c90c98852ec1fe00db9ad366a23827497efea43a951de2ff9c3a85.png)

You could absolutely spin up a VPS on Digital Ocean for $7 / month. It'll be your custom file system + bash. You could even run [clawd.bot](https://clawd.bot) in it so you can directly talk to it via Telegram or phone call. But vps is expensive. If it's a record label with one employee, maybe that's fine. If you're a record label with 10+ employees, giving each a clawd.bot is now $70 / month. As clawd.bot runs, it fills more and more of your memory, especially if it's running non-stop, all the time. Now you need to worry about

*   Pruning memory.
    
*   Restarting the vps when (not if) there's an error that crashes your server.
    
*   Dev ops for new server upgrades.
    
*   etc.
    

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/3e4e83b215694b27b369f6a9dfa7b58b4d115667f62e59cf65325a4a6900dea3.png)

Sandbox is just-in-time compute when and how you need it. Each prompt can specify a new

*   Resources.
    
*   Time alive.
    
*   Runtime.
    
*   File system image.
    

This makes the sandboxes for your record label flexible to help you keep costs low and iteration speed fast for any new changes you and your team need to make to daily label operations.

title: Open Labels
author: sweetman
excerpt: The record label is no longer a set of tools. It’s a programmable system your agent can run. hello world
body:
Today we're announcing Recoup Sandboxes. Sandboxes are a rearchitecture of Recoup, with a shared file system and Bash for each label. A sandbox provides an environment where an agent can run code, store files, and work within configured runtime, storage, and access limits. Connected workflows can help move information between tools—for example, preparing audience information for a release document when the required data access and integrations are configured.

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/e661461336733bca760fcbf9ecc00547c19f0be3494f654e2a1f14daa34b2aaf.png)

The current web app ([app.recoupable.dev](https://app.recoupable.dev)) was built over 18+ months ago. We started building Recoup when the [AI SDK](https://ai-sdk.dev/) was first released. Web chat was still in its early days. We were building chats that knew what artist you selected and showed Tool UI Components based. We ran into a few core issues along the way.

Before

*   Leaving the tab → lost progress
    
*   Custom file system → bugs + maintenance
    
*   MCP tools → limited access
    

Now

*   Durable workflows → resumable work
*   Sandboxes → isolated file systems
*   Bash → command-line tools and integrations within the environment’s permissions and limits

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/6d599c3c61a0640bcabeb2109401aae8edd64bd7d5e9a131403bfbabd3831e68.png)

Legacy: Create new artist

Agents can use durable workflows and cloud environments to keep work separate from a browser session. Recoup sandboxes are a fork of [Open Agents by Vercel](https://vercel.com/templates/template/open-agents), a framework for long-lived agent workflows. The architecture brings together:

* Workflows — resumable steps within the service’s runtime and usage limits.
* Sandboxes — isolated file systems for label work.
* Bash — command-line access to tools and resources permitted by the environment.

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/f29e5f630e52a6f0236df3b5a4335b8b0282fd914ddc38c0cb2d87e118ea06e9.png)

A connected workflow might retrieve an available asset or use permitted Chartmetric data to prepare an update to a release document. The available sources, data freshness, and write access depend on the integrations and credentials in the setup. Review the result before relying on it or sharing it with the team.

**Start here →** [https://app.recoupable.dev](https://app.recoupable.dev)

**Build with OpenClaw →** [https://docs.recoupable.dev](https://docs.recoupable.dev)

Sandboxes are still evolving, and some integrations require API keys or setup—but the core workflow is live today.

title: Bring your own agent
author: sweetman
excerpt: Nobody wants to visit your web chat.
body:
2 years ago, when we started building [Recoup](https://recoupable.dev/), **most record labels did not have an AI strategy**. We built the Recoup web UI to focus 90% of attention as the first, and only, point of contact between record label team members and AI. We helped record label team members to mix AI with the APIs needed to do their job like Spotify, YouTube, and web search. We built a chat so record label team members could try out any model, get the best features from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Grok, and spend less time on the boring parts of building a record label.

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/7082d55c9e32937936233e54b415853b8cb265f5ecd6abad23af5dc0251a2e66.png)

Recoup Web Chat

Today, every record label is asking how they can continue to scale without increasing head count. Musicians use [Claude Cowork](https://www.anthropic.com/product/claude-cowork) to generate content from all the images on their computer instead of sitting in front of a camera all day. Managers have [OpenAI Codex](https://openai.com/codex/) to update release documents and sync them with Google Drive. Everyone has their own [Openclaw](https://openclaw.ai/). **Nobody wants to visit your website to chat with AI**. Your web chat is inferior to the agents musicians already because your web chat

*   Can't access local file systems on a laptop (most important difference).
    
*   Lacks the personality and memory of a personal assistant.
    
*   Has bugs that make it frustrating to use.
    

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/09932d871330402b0cb025514036eb3022229c8dc971dfc609ba6cebac1379de.png)

Claude Cowork with Recoup Plugins

We've decided it doesn't make sense to fight the trend of `bring your own agent`. Recoup was never going to be the best AI chat interface. We only built the web UI to support the reality that existed in 2024, when the only way to access ChatGPT was to visit the website. Instead, we've decided to lean in to this trend by **making it as easy as possible for personal agents to use Recoup to fill in the gaps needed to build a record label.**

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/2e934f22e7aba8746cb1513a2d44b788c181a0c9d671deceb0fd6960394df519.png)

Recoup Docs can be read by any LLM

**Recoup offers a single, free, API key to give your agent(s) the most accurate, verbose, realtime data across the music industry.** A personal agent can search the web, but general web search is inaccurate compared to [Chartmetric's](https://chartmetric.com/) realtime data for playlist, streaming and audience data. A personal agent can make an image but it can't lookup the performance latest reels on Instagram to create viral hits that match existing style. A personal agent can setup tasks as long as your laptop is powered on, but doesn't know how to monitor your latest releases across social and streaming platforms in realtime to proactively manage release campaigns while you sleep.

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/papyrus_images/fe0e1235dcd9d8c78997452787d5a331f58ee662b1062dd3d598f0c71f9aa340.png)

While Recoup still looks the same today as it did yesterday, we'll be updating the web apps over the coming weeks. The main change you'll see is `less web chat` and `more bring your own agent`. Instead of forcing you to use our web chat, we'll be focusing the web UI on helping make your personal, local, assistant more capable of helping build a record label. If you want to turbo charge your personal agent with the best tools for the music industry, Recoup has the tools you need including

*   Docs any LLM can easily read to get set up: [Docs](https://docs.recoupable.dev/)
    
*   Simple setup for Claude Code / Codex / OpenClaw / Hermes: [Agents](https://docs.recoupable.dev/agents)
    
*   Marketplaces and Plugins to run your record label: [Marketplaces](https://github.com/recoupable/marketplace)
    

If you need help, please reach out to us at agent@recoupable.dev.
